 US central bank keeps interest rates unchanged in final decision before midterm elections
 28 October 2026 Summary
 We've concluded our live coverage for today. You can read more here: US central bank holds interest rates steady ahead of midterm elections – here's what that means 
 The US central bank has left interest rates unchanged in its final decision before the US midterm elections 
 Last month, the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years to 3.75%-4%, hinting at additional hikes this year to help curb inflation 
 Today's decision was not unanimous with two of the 12 board members voting to raise rates
 President Trump strongly opposes interest rate hikes and pushed for a quick cut following the bank's September decision
 Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said despite "geopolitical developments" the US economy is resilient but inflation remains elevated
 "Politics played no role in the decision" to maintain rates, he added when asked about the upcoming elections
 What are interest rates and why should you care? 
 Close form Do you have questions about the US midterm elections?
 Get in touch Live Reporting
 Edited by Sakshi Venkatraman with business reporter Rachel Clun in New York
 US central bank remains concerned about prices published at 20:17 GMT 20:17 GMT 
 Here's what we learned today: 
 The US Federal Reserve has held steady interest rates at 3.75%-4%, a month after its Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates for the first time in three years
 Unlike last month, two out of the 12-member committee voted to increase rates
 Fed chair Kevin Warsh says while employment levels remain positive, the US central bank remains concerned about price rises
 "Inflation is too high" for American households he says, adding that the bank will work to "deliver price stability"
 Stable prices means keeping inflation near its target of 2%. Raising or lowering interest rates is the Fed’s main tool for getting inflation to that target
 Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. On the flip side, it also means interest rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise
 Warsh says the imminent US midterm elections - often characterised as an appraisal of the current administration - did not play a part in the bank's decision to hold rates.
 We're ending our live coverage now, but you can read more about the Fed's decision and what it means for the US economy here: US central bank holds interest rates steady ahead of midterm elections – here's what that means

 No dose of ‘monetary medicine’ this month – nor a hint of what will come next published at 20:06 GMT 20:06 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 According to Fed chair Kevin Warsh, inflation may be high,
and the economy is strong, but there are other signs - such as tightening credit
conditions - that things are moving in the right direction.
 “The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is
that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some,” he
said, referring to last month’s interest rate rise.
 There is also plenty more economic data to come between now
and the committee’s next meeting starting on 8 December, he said, which should
paint a more detailed picture of the state of the economy.
 At that point, he said, “we’ll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right
policy decision and the stance of policy."
 While last month the committee signalled there could be one
more rate rise this year, Warsh would not be drawn on where he thinks they will
go in six weeks’ time.
 “A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to
share with you my musings.”

 Why are prices rising for Americans? published at 19:48 GMT 19:48 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 Inflation has been rising largely to due to higher fuel prices, which in turn have been driven up by the cost of oil.
 Vehicle fuel prices have jumped by 34.2% over 12 months, and rose by 9.1% in September alone, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation according to the Bureau of Labour Statistics.
 Energy inflation was also up by 20.4% over the year, with prices for home heating oil, energy services and electricity climbing. 
 These steep increases are thanks to high oil prices, which since February have been impacted by the war with Iran. The global benchmark, brent crude, has been above $110 a barrel since 22 October, well above the pre-war level of about $70 a barrel.

 On the economy, ominous signs brewing for Trump ahead of midterms published at 19:38 GMT 19:38 GMT 
 Bernd Debusmann Jr 
White House reporter 
 With just days left to go until the midterms here in the US, Donald Trump's approval ratings on the economy have hit new lows - potentially a troubling sign for Republicans that are on the ballot across the country. 
 A recent, economy-specific poll by CNBC found that about eight out of 10 Americans view the economy as fair, or poor, about the same number as during the end of the Covid-19 pandemic. 
 The poll found that just over 63% of Americans are pessimistic about how things stand, including 35% of Republican voters - the highest figure in both of Trump's administrations. 
 In what may well be another troubling sign for Republican candidates, a significant number of Democrats - 72% - say they are highly interested in the midterms, compared to 62% of Republicans. 
 Interest rates themselves aren't on the ballot - and are set by the Federal Reserve - but the overall sentiment regarding the US economy is poor, and many voters will hope their their votes result in a Congress next year that can adopt policies they believe will help. 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, US President Donald Trump attends a midterm election rally to support Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, in Lubbock, Texas

 Fed considering change in how it decides interest rates published at 19:23 GMT 19:23 GMT 
 Michelle Fleury 
New York business correspondent 
 The US Federal Reserve is considering a significant change to how it makes interest-rate decisions.
 The central bank plans to reduce the number of interest rate setting meetings to seven next year and six in 2028, down from its usual eight meetings a year.
 The idea is to use that extra time to step back and take a broader look at monetary policy and the economy.
 That could give policymakers more time to assess the data and see the bigger picture. But there’s also a potential trade-off: with fewer scheduled meetings, the Fed could have less flexibility to respond quickly if the economy takes an unexpected turn.
 And this isn’t completely out of left field. Fed Governor Kevin Warsh raised the possibility of fewer policy meetings over the summer.
 Image caption, The US Federal Reserve Building in Washington DC

 What does the decision to leave rates unchanged mean for you? published at 19:14 GMT 19:14 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 The Fed uses interest rate changes to try to improve the
economy: the central bank’s main aims are to maximise jobs and keep prices stable.
 Stable prices means keeping inflation near its
target of 2%.
 Raising or lowering interest rates is the Fed’s main tool
for getting inflation to that target.
 Those changes normally flow through to other interest rates
set by commercial banks and other institutions, which in turn affects spending
and saving decisions from households and businesses.
 Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new
mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. On the flip side, it also means interest
rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise.
 Read more about how the Fed works and what interest rate changes mean here .

 Fed chair concludes remarks published at 19:09 GMT 19:09 GMT 
 Kevin Warsh's news conference has ended but stay with us as we bring you analysis from our business team on today's interest rates decision and what it may mean for the US economy and upcoming midterm elections.

 'Politics played no role in the decision' says Warsh published at 19:06 GMT 19:06 GMT 
 Image source, Reuters A reporter asks Warsh how much politics and the upcoming 3 November midterm election played in the Fed's decision not to raise rates.
 Inflation and the cost of living are key issues for American voters.
 "Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh says. 
 In the two days the board had its discussion, there wasn't one mention of politics or the upcoming election, he adds.

 Warsh won't respond to Trump comments on Fed board composition published at 19:03 GMT 19:03 GMT 
 Warsh is reminded about recent comments by Trump suggesting the Fed board's bipartisan makeup means there are people on it that "would like to see the country do badly in my opinion".
 The Fed chair is asked if he agrees with those comments.
 But Warsh says he wouldn't respond to statements made by Trump or other public officials.
 "We came to the right policy decision for this moment and I am honoured to be here and honoured to be the chairman of this group," he says.

 Trump's adamant opposition to raising interest rates published at 18:58 GMT 18:58 GMT 
 Image source, EPA The US president has been clear in no uncertain terms that he wants to see interest rates in the US lowered. 
 While it’s not his decision to make (that falls to the central bank), it hasn’t stopped Trump from making his views heard. 
 After the Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023, Trump took to social media to demand a lower rate. 
 "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he said. "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Warsh asked why rates were not raised today published at 18:48 GMT 18:48 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Reporters are now asking Warsh questions. 
 One asks the Fed chair if the group is inching towards raising rates in December, why not raise rates today? 
 Warsh says that "quashing inflation" is not about a specific date or data point, but rather about the broader objectives and a monetary policy strategy. 
 He says there's a lot that's happening in the world before the next meeting and he will be watching to see what happens globally. 
 "We're working on it," Warsh says. 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'It's our responsibility to get inflation down' says Warsh published at 18:42 GMT 18:42 GMT 
 High tech investment is leading US economic acceleration and the jobless rate is lower than a year ago, Warsh says.
 The Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices. On the jobs side of its goals, Warsh says that is looking "quite positive".
 But on the price side, he reiterates that "inflation is too high" for American households.
 "Americans, of course, are still dealing inflation that has been running above the committee's objective for close to six years," he says. "It's our responsibility to get inflation down."
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Warsh says Fed 'will deliver price stability' published at 18:36 GMT 18:36 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Fed chair Kevin Warsh is now speaking to the media, following his remarks he's expected to take questions from reporters. 
 He says the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) maintained the rate, but cautioned that the financial uncertainty remains due to "geopolitical developments".
 Warsh says the economy is resilient, but notes that inflation remains elevated. 
 "The committee will deliver price stability," he added.

 Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh to address the media published at 18:25 GMT 18:25 GMT 
 Fed chair Kevin Warsh is set to hold a news conference in a few minutes.
 He will answer questions from reporters who are likely to ask about the committee's decision to keep rates as they are - and about the overall health of the US economy.
 We will bring you his most important lines here.

 How the federal interest rate has changed over the last five years published at 18:20 GMT 18:20 GMT 
 The US central bank increased interest rates last month for the first time since 2023.
 Another increase is widely expected later this year.

 US economy resilient despite uncertainty, central bank says published at 18:16 GMT 18:16 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 In its news release justifying why it held the interest rate steady, the Federal Reserve acknowledged that inflation remains high. 
 But it also said it wants to gather more information on how best to bring it down. 
 “The committee will deliver price stability,” it said.
 The Fed noted that while there was uncertainty, the US
economy remained resilient.
 “Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the committee
said. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the
unemployment rate has changed little."

 Decision to hold rates steady was not unanimous published at 18:07 GMT 18:07 GMT 
 Rachel Clun 
Business reporter 
 The decision to hold rates steady today was not unanimous.
 While 10 of the 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep rates
unchanged, two voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%, from
its current 3.75%-4%.
 The Fed increased rates last month for the first time in three years, and it is anticipated to raise them again before the year is over.

 The US Federal Reserve has announced it will hold interest rates steady at 3.75%-4%.

 Two potential reasons for rising prices in the US published at 17:53 GMT 17:53 GMT 
 Michelle Fleury 
New York business correspondent 
 Image source, Getty Images Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of Trump’s own policies, including tariffs, and the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.
 "The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans. "It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."
 Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.
 A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.
 The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.
 Conflict with Iran has pushed global oil prices higher, lifted the cost of petrol at home and put fresh pressure on household budgets.

 What is the interest rate and why should you care? published at 17:43 GMT 17:43 GMT 
 Sakshi Venkatraman 
Live editor 
 Many American voters have affordability on their minds right now. But what can the central bank do about it? 
 The Federal Reserve, or Fed, helps set borrowing costs across the economy, by deciding what to charge banks to borrow through its interest rate range. 
 When it increases that key interest rate target, consumer banks typically follow with similar moves, making the cost of borrowing and taking out loans more expensive for everyone. That means higher monthly payments on debt like credit cards and car loans for Americans. 
 It also can drive up interest rates for Treasuries - which in turn in turn increase the rates charged for mortgages.
 However higher interest rates can benefit savers, through higher rates of returns on deposits.
